anti_patterns: Assuming L2 soft-confirmations are final: building irreversible L1 actions on unchallenged sequencer output instead of waiting for the challenge window or buying finality from a liquidity provider
Running no independent verifier: trusting the sequencer's state roots while nobody re-executes batches, which voids the 1-of-N-honest assumption the whole design rests on
Skipping the forced-inclusion path: leaving users with only the sequencer mempool so a censoring sequencer can freeze accounts with no L1 deposit escape hatch

Treating the dispute game as free insurance: posting assertions without bonded challengers, monitoring (op-dispute-mon equivalents), or gas budgets, then discovering during an attack that nobody can afford to defend

Deploying custom dispute parameters without review: changing bond sizes, game depth, or challenge clocks (op-deployer's dangerouslyAllowCustomDisputeParameters) without the economic analysis that prices delay and spam attacks
Ignoring L1 reorgs in derivation: advancing the safe head from unfinalized L1 data so a beacon reorg silently rewinds what clients treated as settled L2 history
avoid_when: Withdrawals or cross-chain actions need L1 finality in minutes rather than ~7 days
The application is a low-throughput CRUD system where L1 fees are already acceptable
No party is willing to run a verifier and fund challenge bonds, leaving assertions unchallenged by default
Strict data-residency or permissioning rules forbid posting transaction data to a public L1
benefits: 10-100x throughput over L1 with near-EVM-equivalent execution: existing contracts and tooling (a Geth fork in Arbitrum Nitro, the OP Stack execution client) run almost unchanged
L1-grade security under a 1-of-N honesty assumption: a single honest watcher re-executing posted batches can defeat any number of malicious asserters through the fraud-proof game

Cheap fraud proving: watchers run ordinary L2 nodes rather than specialized provers, and disputes resolve through interactive bisection down to one verifiable step instead of re-executing whole batches on L1
Censorship-resistant liveness: users can force transaction inclusion via L1 deposits (OptimismPortal / delayed inbox), so a censoring sequencer can delay but not freeze accounts
EIP-4844 blob pricing: batch data posts to the independent blob-fee lane instead of execution calldata, cutting the dominant operating cost
best_practices: Run at least one independent watchtower verifier plus dispute monitoring from day one, with bonded capital and gas budgets sized for an attack, not the happy path
Keep the Guardian / Security Council backstop (pause withdrawals, blacklist bad games, fall back to a permissioned game) until permissionless validation has survived real challenges
Post batches as EIP-4844 blobs where supported and pass through the dynamic L1-data fee so batch-poster costs stay covered as blob gas moves
Size assertion and challenge bonds above the opportunity cost of a week-long delay on total bridged value, and use a liquid, low-volatility bonding asset
Rehearse sequencer failover (Raft leader transfer drills for op-conductor style clusters) and dispute response (spurious challenge) before mainnet value arrives
Track L1 finality separately from L2 derivation: mark derived blocks safe only from finalized L1 data, and label output-root finality (post-challenge-window) distinctly from PoS finality
component_types: Sequencer / Batcher: orders L2 transactions, builds blocks, compresses batches into channels/frames and posts them to the L1 data-availability layer
L1 Bridge Contracts (OptimismPortal / Arbitrum Inbox and Bridge): escrow L1 assets, accept deposits for forced inclusion, record asserted state/output roots
Proposer / Asserter: bonds capital and posts claims about L2 state (output roots) to the dispute-game factory on a fixed interval
Challenger / Watcher (op-challenger, Arbitrum watchtower validator): re-executes batches locally and opens interactive disputes against invalid assertions
Dispute Game Contracts (FaultDisputeGame / BoLD ChallengeManager, OneStepProof verifier): run the bisection protocol and execute the single-step proof on L1, slashing the loser
Derivation Pipeline (rollup node): reconstructs the canonical L2 chain purely from L1 data so any verifier converges without trusting the sequencer
Guardian / Security Council: backstop role that can pause withdrawals, blacklist games, or revert to a permissioned game on failure
context: Ethereum L1 processes roughly 15-30 TPS with volatile gas fees, which prices out high-volume applications (payments, trading, gaming, social) while remaining the most secure and decentralized settlement layer available. An optimistic rollup moves execution off-chain onto an L2 chain that posts its compressed transaction batches to L1 for data availability and records claimed state roots in L1 bridge contracts. The claims are accepted optimistically: anyone may challenge a root inside a dispute window (about 7 days on OP Mainnet and Arbitrum One), triggering an interactive fraud-proof game in which the asserter and challenger bisect the disputed execution down to a single step that an L1 contract re-executes to identify the liar, whose bond is slashed. Security therefore rests on L1 consensus plus data availability plus the liveness of at least one honest watcher, rather than on re-executing every transaction on L1.
design_principles: Optimistic acceptance with bonded claims: assert first, prove only on dispute, and make every claim slashable
Derivability from L1 data alone: any party reading only the parent chain must converge on the same L2 history without trusting the operator
One-honest-party sufficiency: the protocol must let a single honest bonded participant defeat arbitrarily many adversaries within a bounded delay
Separation of soft and hard finality: fast sequencer preconfirmations for UX, L1-anchored derivation for ordering finality, post-challenge-window roots for withdrawal finality
Deterministic replay: the L2 state-transition function must be exactly reproducible (Nitro WASM, Cannon MIPS) so one-step proofs are decidable on L1

technology_stack: OP Stack (op-node, op-batcher, op-proposer, op-challenger, Cannon fault-proof VM)
Arbitrum Nitro and BoLD dispute contracts
EIP-4844 blob-carrying transactions for batch data availability
L1 bridge and dispute-game contracts (OptimismPortal, DisputeGameFactory, Rollup, ChallengeManager)
tradeoffs: Slow L1 finality: withdrawals must wait out the ~7-day challenge window (plus dispute resolution and safety delays), unlike ZK rollups with immediate validity proofs
Challenge-liveness assumption: safety depends on at least one honest watcher staying online, funded, and uncensored on L1 for the whole window

Sequencer centralization in practice: most deployments run a single (or operator-cluster) sequencer, so short-term liveness and ordering fairness depend on the operator plus the forced-inclusion hatch
Dispute capital costs: permissionless validation requires large bonds (e.g. thousands of ETH-class assertion bonds on Arbitrum One) and gas budgets for bisection moves
Operator complexity: sequencer, batcher, proposer, challenger, monitors, and upgrade Guardians must be run, funded, and rehearsed as one system
L1 data cost floor: every L2 transaction still pays amortized L1 batch-posting fees, so throughput gains track blob/calldata pricing
use_cases: EVM-compatible DeFi and payments at 10-100x L1 throughput with L1-anchored settlement (OP Mainnet, Arbitrum One, Base)
High-volume consumer apps (gaming, social, activity feeds) needing sub-second sequencer confirmations with eventual L1 finality
App-chains launching via the OP Stack or Arbitrum Orbit with a working fault-proof system and HA sequencer cluster from day one
Bridged-asset ecosystems where users accept a 7-day withdrawal delay in exchange for full EVM equivalence without specialized provers
